case.title: BRAF V600E right-sided colon cancer with initially unresectable bilobar liver metastases after major early response to encorafenib/cetuximab/mFOLFOX6
case.primary_mdt_question: Has systemic treatment converted the hepatic disease to a state in which curative-intent local therapy is justified now, or should systemic treatment continue to establish deeper and more durable disease control?

patient.living_situation: lives with partner; two adult children
goals: maximize probability of long-term disease control or cure
accept substantial short-term toxicity if curative intent is credible
strong preference to preserve independence and avoid permanent stoma

comorbidities.status: HbA1c 48 mmol/mol; no established neuropathy or nephropathy

comorbidities.condition: provoked left popliteal DVT after ankle fracture

family_history.sibling: sister with advanced adenoma at age 61

baseline_medications: metformin XR 1000 mg PO with evening meal
paracetamol 1000 mg PO up to three times daily PRN
oral ferrous fumarate initially prescribed; stopped after IV iron

segment 8 lesion approaches the right anterior portal pedicle

primary_colon_biopsy.lymphovascular_invasion: cannot be reliably assessed in superficial biopsy

initial_mdt_assessment.treatment_goal: systemic disease control with explicit reassessment for curative-intent local treatment
controversies:
contemporary BRAF-targeted first-line therapy versus a conversion-focused FOLFOXIRI/bevacizumab strategy
whether the 5 mm lung nodule should prevent a liver-only curative strategy
whether early colectomy adds anything when the asymptomatic liver burden is the life-limiting component

systemic_regimen.name: encorafenib + cetuximab + mFOLFOX6
systemic_regimen.rationale: selected after molecular confirmation of BRAF V600E mutation, with explicit reassessment for conversion

regimen_details.fluorouracil: mFOLFOX6 bolus/46-hour infusion per institutional protocol

vascular_relationship_changes.S4a: major reduction; now approximately 2 mm from the middle hepatic vein without circumferential involvement

liver_MRI.radiology_conclusion: substantial response; all currently visible hepatic deposits appear potentially clearable by combined parenchymal-sparing resection and thermal ablation in an expert hepatobiliary unit

ctDNA.interpretation: major molecular response but persistent detectable ctDNA

current_resectability_review.HPB_surgeon_opinion: conversion from technically unresectable to potentially completely locally treatable disease
proposed_liver_strategy: segment 4a wedge/resection with middle hepatic vein preservation if possible
thermal ablation of selected deep segment 6, 3 and 1 lesions
intraoperative ultrasound to identify chemotherapy-altered/disappearing lesions

alternative_if_S1_or_S4a_not_safely_clea: additional systemic therapy with subsequent reassessment
colon_strategy_options: synchronous right hemicolectomy if hepatic procedure remains limited
continue systemic therapy and defer colectomy

alternatives: multifocal benign lesions: inconsistent with MRI/PET and treatment response

primary_histology: medullary carcinoma unlikely given morphology and pMMR phenotype

unresolved_mdt_questions:
Is four cycles enough evidence of systemic disease control to interrupt a highly active first-line regimen for liver surgery?
Does persistent low-level ctDNA argue against immediate metastasectomy, or does it simply reflect still-visible metastatic disease?
Should a stable 5 mm pulmonary nodule be treated as presumed M1b disease and therefore lower enthusiasm for curative liver surgery?
Should the colon primary be removed synchronously, after liver surgery, or only after additional demonstration of disease control?
Is a combined resection/ablation strategy oncologically equivalent enough to justify avoiding a major hepatectomy?
What duration of perioperative BRAF/EGFR-targeted treatment is reasonable when prospective perioperative data are sparse?

management_alternatives.name: **Conversion strategy: move to liver-directed curative-intent treatment now**
management_alternatives.sequence: Hold systemic treatment → expert parenchymal-sparing metastasectomies plus ablation of deep lesions → short-interval CT/ctDNA → staged right hemicolectomy if no progression → individualized postoperative systemic therapy.
management_alternatives.advantages: Exploits the present window of technical resectability; minimizes additional oxaliplatin-related neuropathy and chemotherapy-associated liver injury; removes all radiographically visible dominant metastatic disease; provides hepatic pathology and treatment-response information.
management_alternatives.disadvantages: Four cycles may be too short a “test of time” for biologically aggressive BRAF-mutant cancer; persistent ctDNA and the lung nodule could represent occult systemic disease; there is no randomized trial specifically validating hepatectomy after BREAKWATER therapy.
management_alternatives.evidence: CAIRO5 validates repeated conversion assessment and local-treatment intent in initially unresectable CRLM, while BREAKWATER validates the systemic regimen—but the two evidence streams have not been prospectively combined. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified]

management_alternatives.name: **Systemic-control strategy: continue EC + mFOLFOX6 for another two to four cycles before surgery**
management_alternatives.sequence: Continue current regimen → repeat CT/MRI and ctDNA after approximately 8–12 additional weeks → operate only if no new disease and all lesions remain clearable.
management_alternatives.advantages: Provides a stronger biological test of disease control; could deepen response and clarify the lung nodule; retains an evidence-based BRAF-directed first-line treatment that has demonstrated superior PFS/OS to standard therapy.
management_alternatives.disadvantages: Potential loss of surgical window if resistant clones emerge; increasing neuropathy and liver injury; lesions can become difficult to identify after deep radiological response; persistent chemotherapy exposure may add toxicity without improving curability.
management_alternatives.evidence: BREAKWATER phase III evidence strongly supports systemic efficacy. The unanswered question is optimal duration before conversion surgery. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified]

management_alternatives.name: **Disease-control strategy: defer major surgery and prioritize systemic treatment with selective local consolidation**
management_alternatives.sequence: Continue targeted systemic therapy; reserve ablation/SBRT for a threatening or oligoresidual lesion; resect primary only for symptoms or later strategic consolidation.
management_alternatives.advantages: Lowest immediate operative burden; acknowledges the systemic biology of BRAF-mutant stage IV CRC; avoids a large multistep surgical program whose survival benefit is uncertain.
management_alternatives.disadvantages: May forfeit a rare curative-intent opportunity after genuine conversion; systemic therapy alone is not synonymous with cure; local treatment later may become anatomically impossible.
management_alternatives.evidence: Supported indirectly by the CAIRO5 long-term caution that more response/local treatment does not inherently guarantee survival improvement and by contemporary systemic efficacy data. It is not evidence that potentially curable liver-only disease should never be operated. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified]

specialty_contributions.interpretation: Excellent early response to a contemporary BRAF-directed regimen, with a >80% CEA reduction and major plasma-VAF fall, but persistent measurable and molecular disease.
specialty_contributions.contribution: Decide whether four cycles provide sufficient systemic “test of time”; define perioperative interruption/restart strategy; balance further oxaliplatin exposure against the risk of delaying a window for complete local treatment. BREAKWATER supports the regimen's systemic efficacy, but did not specifically establish a conversion-hepatectomy pathway. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified]

specialty_contributions.interpretation: Baseline disease was not safely treatable by conventional major resection; response has created a plausible parenchymal-sparing clearance strategy.
specialty_contributions.contribution: Confirm every original lesion can be addressed, including radiologically regressed lesions; use intraoperative ultrasound; determine one-stage versus staged liver clearance; protect adequate remnant liver and hepatic venous drainage. CAIRO5 demonstrates the importance of repeated expert surgical review. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified]

specialty_contributions.interpretation: Primary remains nonobstructing and therefore has not forced the treatment sequence.
specialty_contributions.contribution: Compare liver-first, synchronous and staged colectomy. A liver-first approach minimizes interruption of management of the organ currently driving prognosis; synchronous surgery decreases total procedures but raises operative complexity.

specialty_contributions.interpretation: Imaging now suggests technically treatable disease, but the segment 1/IVC and segment 4a/MHV interfaces remain the principal anatomical risks. The 5-mm lung nodule cannot be reliably adjudicated by baseline PET.
specialty_contributions.contribution: Side-by-side baseline/current lesion mapping; liver volumetry; identify “disappearing” metastases; specifically document vessel distance and whether every baseline focus remains targetable.

specialty_contributions.interpretation: Several deep lesions may be better treated by thermal ablation than by sacrificing major liver parenchyma.
specialty_contributions.contribution: Define safe ablation margins and whether lesions next to the IVC are susceptible to heat-sink or access limitations. DEBIR90Y is an interventional approach to liver-dominant CRC, although that phase I strategy itself showed considerable toxicity and limited overall response and is not a preferred solution for this potentially resectable patient. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified]

specialty_contributions.interpretation: Radiation is not the preferred method for clearing nine widespread liver lesions when surgical/ablative clearance is achievable, but it is valuable as a contingency for one anatomically unsafe residual focus.
specialty_contributions.contribution: Assess SBRT or MR-guided treatment particularly for the segment 1/IVC or segment 4a/MHV lesion if neither resection nor thermal ablation can achieve an acceptable local treatment.

specialty_contributions.interpretation: The phenotype is unequivocally colorectal and BRAF V600E-driven, pMMR/MSS, RAS wild type and HER2-negative.
specialty_contributions.contribution: Review tumor heterogeneity; preserve tissue from any hepatic resection for treatment-effect assessment and research; compare metastatic molecular profile if unexpected progression occurs.

specialty_contributions.interpretation: “Palliative care” here means symptom and decision support, not abandonment of curative intent.
specialty_contributions.contribution: Manage fatigue, rash, neuropathy, iron deficiency and uncertainty; establish how the patient values a substantial surgical burden against uncertain cure probability; ensure goals are revisited if extrahepatic disease declares itself.

narrative:
## Full case MDT case dossier **Use case:** advanced colorectal-cancer MDT / conversion-to-resectability simulation. **Primary learning question:** *Does a major early molecular and radiological response in BRAF V600E metastatic colon cancer justify moving from systemic treatment to curative-intent local therapy when the evidence supporting the systemic regimen and the evidence supporting conversion surgery come from different trial populations?* The choice of BRAF-mutant, liver-dominant CRC connects CAIRO5's conversion framework, PLCRC-style biomarker research and current biomarker-directed systemic therapy. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] The initial systemic choice is deliberately debatable. BREAKWATER provides phase III evidence for first-line encorafenib–cetuximab plus mFOLFOX6 in BRAF V600E metastatic CRC, and the Dutch NVMO listed encorafenib/cetuximab/chemotherapy in its July 2026 advice. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] Yet the patient phenotype—**right-sided/BRAF-mutant, liver-only or nearly liver-only, initially unresectable but potentially convertible disease**—is also almost tailor-made for the clinical question addressed by CAIRO5, whose original analysis favored FOLFOXIRI–bevacizumab for this biological group. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] The persistent ctDNA after a large imaging response is intentionally provocative rather than diagnostically decisive. PROVENC3 concerns ctDNA as a powerful prognostic marker, but that study involved resected stage III colon cancer rather than metastatic patients undergoing conversion therapy; its hazard ratios therefore cannot simply be transplanted into this patient's peri-hepatectomy decision. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] **Suggested images immediately after the dossier:** A case four-panel radiology plate would work especially well: axial portal-venous CT at baseline showing the 48-mm segment 8 and 36-mm segment 4a lesions; hepatobiliary-phase gadoxetate MRI showing all nine deposits; matched post-treatment MRI demonstrating shrinkage; and a 3-D liver map showing lesions, portal/hepatic veins, IVC and proposed resection/ablation zones. A second figure should plot CEA and ctDNA on a logarithmic scale against treatment cycles. A third could be an oncoprint showing **BRAF V600E / APC / TP53 / SMAD4**, MSS/pMMR status and the absence of RAS/HER2/NTRK alterations. These should be explicitly watermarked **case — NOT CLINICAL IMAGING**. ## MDT interpretation, specialty positions and competing management plans The current MDT should not reduce the question to “is the liver technically operable?” The more informative formulation is: > **Has treatment transformed this patient from unresectable stage IV disease into a biological state in which complete local clearance has a credible chance of producing durable disease control?** CAIRO5 is highly pertinent because resectability was repeatedly reviewed by a liver expert panel using predefined criteria, precisely recognizing that resectability is dynamic rather than a one-time staging label. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] The important warning from its longer-term analysis is that **higher response and more aggressive cytoreduction cannot automatically be assumed to improve survival**, which should temper enthusiasm for equating an impressive scan with proof of curability. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] ### Specialty-specific MDT contributions | Specialty | Interpretation | Specific MDT contribution | |---|---|---| | **Medical oncology** | Excellent early response to a contemporary BRAF-directed regimen, with a >80% CEA reduction and major plasma-VAF fall, but persistent measurable and molecular disease. | Decide whether four cycles provide sufficient systemic “test of time”; define perioperative interruption/restart strategy; balance further oxaliplatin exposure against the risk of delaying a window for complete local treatment. BREAKWATER supports the regimen's systemic efficacy, but did not specifically establish a conversion-hepatectomy pathway. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] | | **Hepatobiliary surgery** | Baseline disease was not safely treatable by conventional major resection; response has created a plausible parenchymal-sparing clearance strategy. | Confirm every original lesion can be addressed, including radiologically regressed lesions; use intraoperative ultrasound; determine one-stage versus staged liver clearance; protect adequate remnant liver and hepatic venous drainage. CAIRO5 demonstrates the importance of repeated expert surgical review. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] | | **Colorectal surgery** | Primary remains nonobstructing and therefore has not forced the treatment sequence. | Compare liver-first, synchronous and staged colectomy. A liver-first approach minimizes interruption of management of the organ currently driving prognosis; synchronous surgery decreases total procedures but raises operative complexity. | | **Radiology** | Imaging now suggests technically treatable disease, but the segment 1/IVC and segment 4a/MHV interfaces remain the principal anatomical risks. The 5-mm lung nodule cannot be reliably adjudicated by baseline PET. | Side-by-side baseline/current lesion mapping; liver volumetry; identify “disappearing” metastases; specifically document vessel distance and whether every baseline focus remains targetable. | | **Interventional radiology** | Several deep lesions may be better treated by thermal ablation than by sacrificing major liver parenchyma. | Define safe ablation margins and whether lesions next to the IVC are susceptible to heat-sink or access limitations. DEBIR90Y is an interventional approach to liver-dominant CRC, although that phase I strategy itself showed considerable toxicity and limited overall response and is not a preferred solution for this potentially resectable patient. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] | | **Radiation oncology** | Radiation is not the preferred method for clearing nine widespread liver lesions when surgical/ablative clearance is achievable, but it is valuable as a contingency for one anatomically unsafe residual focus. | Assess SBRT or MR-guided treatment particularly for the segment 1/IVC or segment 4a/MHV lesion if neither resection nor thermal ablation can achieve an acceptable local treatment. | | **Pathology/molecular pathology** | The phenotype is unequivocally colorectal and BRAF V600E-driven, pMMR/MSS, RAS wild type and HER2-negative. | Review tumor heterogeneity; preserve tissue from any hepatic resection for treatment-effect assessment and research; compare metastatic molecular profile if unexpected progression occurs. | | **Palliative/supportive care** | “Palliative care” here means symptom and decision support, not abandonment of curative intent. | Manage fatigue, rash, neuropathy, iron deficiency and uncertainty; establish how the patient values a substantial surgical burden against uncertain cure probability; ensure goals are revisited if extrahepatic disease declares itself. | A central technical point is the **5-mm pulmonary nodule**. It should not be called PET-negative evidence of benignity: a lesion this small is below dependable PET characterization. In the simulation, stability through systemic treatment therefore leaves it genuinely indeterminate. The most defensible MDT behavior is serial thin-section CT rather than falsely resolving uncertainty. A second controversy is **ctDNA**. The approximately 96% fall in case BRAF VAF is biologically reassuring, while persistent positivity is worrying. Yet the relevant evidence base is still disease- and setting-dependent. PROVENC3 strongly supports postoperative ctDNA as a prognostic marker in resected stage III colon cancer, but it also showed that ctDNA-positive status was not synonymous with inevitable recurrence; extrapolating an absolute “do not operate” threshold to conversion-stage IV disease would be scientifically unjustified. The unanswered question is optimal duration before conversion surgery. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] | | **Disease-control strategy: defer major surgery and prioritize systemic treatment with selective local consolidation** | Continue targeted systemic therapy; reserve ablation/SBRT for a threatening or oligoresidual lesion; resect primary only for symptoms or later strategic consolidation. | Lowest immediate operative burden; acknowledges the systemic biology of BRAF-mutant stage IV CRC; avoids a large multistep surgical program whose survival benefit is uncertain. | May forfeit a rare curative-intent opportunity after genuine conversion; systemic therapy alone is not synonymous with cure; local treatment later may become anatomically impossible. | Supported indirectly by the CAIRO5 long-term caution that more response/local treatment does not inherently guarantee survival improvement and by contemporary systemic efficacy data. It is not evidence that potentially curable liver-only disease should never be operated. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] | ### Preferred case MDT position For this **specific fictional patient**, the strongest MDT recommendation would be to **pursue curative-intent local treatment, but only after one final high-quality expert review confirms that every baseline liver site can be mapped and cleared and that repeat thin-slice chest CT shows no convincing pulmonary progression**. The preferred surgical architecture would be liver-first, parenchymal-sparing resection plus selected thermal ablation, rather than a right trisectionectomy requiring a marginal future liver remnant. This conclusion is an MDT inference from the case rather than a guideline-mandated answer. The rationale is that the patient is young and fit, has no proven extrahepatic disease, has experienced substantial systemic, biochemical and molecular response, and has moved from anatomically unresectable to apparently clearable hepatic disease. Conversely, the recommendation should be presented to the patient as **potentially curative rather than predictably curative**, because BRAF V600E biology, persistent ctDNA and the unresolved pulmonary nodule all imply a substantial recurrence risk. The distinction between *technical resectability* and *oncological utility* is the key educational point. A reasonable counter-position is to administer two additional cycles before surgery to strengthen the “test of time.” This is particularly defensible because BREAKWATER showed clear first-line efficacy for the current regimen and because the patient has not yet developed dose-limiting neuropathy. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] The counterargument is that “more response” is not itself a validated surrogate for survival or better local-treatment outcome—one of the lessons emerging from the CAIRO5 program. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] ### MDT decision pathway ```mermaid flowchart TD A["BRAF V600E, pMMR/MSS right-sided colon cancer

This would be especially effective in an MDT app because selecting each date could reveal the corresponding laboratory, imaging or pathology object. ## One-page clinician brief **case patient:** 59-year-old woman, ECOG 1, controlled hypertension/type 2 diabetes, no major frailty. Presented May 2026 with iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, weight loss and mild right-upper-quadrant discomfort. Colonoscopy demonstrated a nonobstructing 5.5-cm ascending-colon adenocarcinoma. **Tumor biology:** moderately-to-poorly differentiated colorectal adenocarcinoma; CK20/CDX2/SATB2 positive; pMMR/MSS; HER2 1+; RAS wild type; **BRAF c.1799T>A p.Val600Glu**; accompanying APC, TP53 and SMAD4 alterations. Baseline CEA 216 µg/L and CA19-9 178 kU/L. Tumor-informed plasma ctDNA strongly positive, BRAF V600E VAF 11.8%. **Baseline extent:** cT3 cN1b cM1a, stage IVA, with nine bilobar liver metastases. Largest lesions were 48 mm in segment 8, 36 mm in segment 4a and 33 mm in segment 7. Segment 4a disease involved the middle-hepatic-vein interface and a segment 1 lesion was only 3 mm from the IVC. Conventional right-trisection strategy would have left an estimated 23% FLR. A 5-mm right-upper-lobe nodule was indeterminate and non-avid on PET but too small for PET to classify reliably. No peritoneal, bone or distant nodal disease. **Initial MDT:** liver metastases technically unresectable but potentially convertible; primary asymptomatic, so no urgent colectomy. The major first-line controversy was BREAKWATER-driven BRAF-targeted therapy versus CAIRO5-style response-maximizing induction. BREAKWATER supports encorafenib–cetuximab plus mFOLFOX6 in first-line BRAF V600E mCRC, whereas the original CAIRO5 analysis supported FOLFOXIRI–bevacizumab for right-sided/RAS/BRAF-mutant initially unresectable CRLM. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] **Treatment received:** four cycles encorafenib + cetuximab + mFOLFOX6. Maximum toxicity: grade 2 acneiform rash, grade 1 sensory neuropathy and grade 2 hypomagnesemia. No febrile neutropenia or major organ toxicity. **Response:** segment 8 metastasis 48→29 mm; segment 4a 36→20 mm; segment 7 33→18 mm. No new lesions. CEA 216→31.6 µg/L. BRAF ctDNA VAF 11.8→0.42%. Lung nodule remains 5 mm. Post-treatment MRI suggests every visible liver focus can now be treated using parenchymal-sparing resection plus thermal ablation. **Central MDT question:** **operate now, continue systemic therapy to establish deeper biological control, or regard the disease as primarily systemic and defer major surgery?** **Arguments for surgery now:** genuine conversion to complete local treatability; fit patient; absence of proven extrahepatic disease; marked radiographic/biochemical/molecular response; avoiding additional cumulative oxaliplatin toxicity; opportunity for potentially curative clearance. **Arguments to wait:** BRAF V600E remains biologically high-risk; ctDNA is still detectable; only four cycles have tested systemic control; 5-mm lung lesion remains unresolved; there is no prospective trial specifically proving the survival value of metastasectomy after BREAKWATER treatment. CAIRO5 long-term findings also caution against assuming that greater response or more local treatment necessarily translates into longer survival. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] **Provisional preferred MDT position:** liver-first curative-intent clearance after repeat expert review and thin-section chest CT, using parenchymal-sparing resection plus ablation rather than major hepatectomy. Delay colectomy until hepatic recovery and confirmation that no systemic escape has occurred. Obtain postoperative pathology and ctDNA, but do **not** use ctDNA alone as an absolute binary criterion for surgery because the best prospective prognostic data, including PROVENC3, derive from a different disease setting. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified] **Key discussion prompts for the app:** 1. Is “technically resectable” sufficient, or must the MDT establish a minimum degree/duration of biological disease control? 2. Would the decision change if the lung nodule grew from 5 to 8 mm while liver disease continued to respond? 3. Should persistent ctDNA after maximal local treatment prompt intensified systemic therapy, a trial, or surveillance? 4. Is combined resection/ablation preferable to a two-stage major hepatectomy in a patient with nine bilobar lesions? 5. Should the asymptomatic primary be removed synchronously, liver-first or last? 6. How should CAIRO5 conversion evidence be reconciled with BREAKWATER's newer BRAF-specific first-line evidence when no head-to-head conversion trial exists? The case requires the MDT to integrate **molecularly selected systemic treatment, longitudinal biomarkers, real-world patient selection, quantitative imaging, repeated liver resectability assessment, quality-of-life considerations and multidisciplinary local therapy rather than treating any one of those domains as sufficient on its own**. The source connects CAIRO/CAIRO3/CAIRO5, PLCRC, ctDNA research and image- and intervention-oriented studies. [Source-supplied reference; not independently verified]
